paper.title: AES Proposal: Rijndael (as standardised in FIPS 197, Advanced Encryption Standard)
paper.venue: AES submission to NIST, 1998 (document version 2, 1999); standard: FIPS 197, NIST, 2001

program.how: written for ounce-core from the algorithm in the paper or specification; no third-party code copied
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf`

claims_checked: AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 with a 128-bit block, written from the algorithm (S-box computed as the GF(2^8) inverse plus the affine map, key expansion, ShiftRows, MixColumns), reproduces all 558 published intermediate states of FIPS 197 Appendix C: 156 + 186 + 216 values for the Cipher, the Inverse Cipher and the Equivalent Inverse Cipher, for key 000102...  and plaintext 00112233...ff

Final ciphertexts 69c4e0d86a7b0430d8cdb78070b4c55a (AES-128), dda97ca4864cdfe06eaf70a0ec0d7191 (AES-192), 8ea2b7ca516745bfeafc49904b496089 (AES-256), and decryption by both inverse ciphers returns the plaintext

expected_values_source.what: FIPS 197 Appendix C (example vectors with every round's intermediate state), which standardises the Rijndael proposal for 128-bit blocks
expected_values_source.note: values extracted from the PDF text by script and compiled in as data; the program was written from the algorithm description. The Rijndael proposal paper itself (which also defines 192- and 256-bit blocks) was not fetched, and none of its block sizes other than 128 bits are checked

negative_control: built with -DAES_AFFINE_C=0x62 (one bit of the S-box affine constant changed), 520 of 558 published values mismatch (the plaintext-independent states do too) and the program exits 1
not_checked: the Rijndael proposal's 192-bit and 256-bit block sizes (only the 128-bit-block AES subset is in FIPS 197)
other key/plaintext pairs: only the single Appendix C key and plaintext per key size are used, no other known-answer sets and no modes of operation
security claims (resistance to differential, linear or other attacks), side-channel behaviour of this table-free but not constant-time code
speed figures (emulator run time says nothing about the authors' hardware)
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: this program, run on ounce-core, produces exactly the 558 intermediate values FIPS 197 publishes for its three example encryptions and both decryption paths. It does not show the security claims hold.
